HOMURA is a **local-first** reader: comics, light novels, PDFs, and image collections can be read once imported. Parsing, pagination, and rendering are all done on your machine, and book content is never uploaded. The desktop app is packaged with Tauri 2, and the same frontend also provides an Android build.

- Current version: **2.2.7**
- Tech stack: Vue 3 + Pinia + Vite 6 + Tauri 2 + TypeScript
- Repository: [Leon-Ning-san/HomuraReader](https://github.com/Leon-Ning-san/HomuraReader)
- Download: [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/Leon-Ning-san/HomuraReader/releases)

## Feature Overview

- **Multi-format bookshelf**: EPUB / KEPUB, CBZ / ZIP comic archives, PDF, MOBI, TXT, Markdown, and image folders.
- **Top-level libraries and favorites**: create, rename, and delete libraries; multi-select to move items in, or move them across libraries. The favorites page shows all favorites in a flat list.
- **Two reading modes**: automatic pagination for novels (including vertical text) and vertical scrolling. For comics: single page, double page, single cover page, and vertical strip.
- **Local progress memory**: saves page number, direction, single/double page mode, font size, font, line spacing, margins, and strip size for each book. Reopening a book resumes automatically.
- **Import and updates**: imports can be canceled, failed imports can be retried, and duplicate names trigger a prompt. Check for, download, and install new versions within the app.
- **Material Design 3**: 10 theme colors and three surfaces (day, eye-care, and night), with separate adaptations for desktop and narrow screens.
- **Offline library**: metadata, covers, original files, and progress all stay on your machine. Nothing is uploaded or synced to the cloud.

An LSPosed module for Honor MagicOS 11 that restores the liquid glass removed by a system update, and takes over the installer, cloud control, SMS, and high-temperature restrictions.

# ESP_TO_SPOOLMAN

NFC filament spool scanner: the device reads an NTAG tag, finds the spool in [Spoolman](https://github.com/Donkie/Spoolman), and sets it as active on the printer via Moonraker (optionally, with gate selection in the Happy Hare MMU). Writing and erasing tags is done by the device itself through its web interface, without third-party applications.

**Tag format: OpenSpool** (`application/json`, `protocol: "openspool"`). FilaMan has dropped out (it moved to a paid model) and is no longer used. Old FilaMan tags can still be read (`sm_id` as a fallback), but when a tag is rewritten, it is fully rewritten in openspool format with data from Spoolman.

## Components used

1. ESP32-C3 super mini controller
2. RFID-RC522 NFC reader
3. WS2812B LED
4. Button
5. NTAG215 and NTAG216 tags (with open writing, meaning no lock bits set)

The project is built for ESP32-C3, but it can be installed on another type of ESP32 by replacing the pins with the corresponding ones. Requires Spoolman **v0.27+** (Tag API) on the local network. For MMU, a printer with Klipper/Moonraker and the Happy Hare + Spoolman integration is required.

# Little Reef

Grow a small seabed with focus time. Each completed focus session makes the seaweed grow a little taller, and now and then a fish, shrimp, or crab comes to visit. This is a quiet desktop focus timer with an aquarium, a visitor field guide, and 20 background sounds.

## Download

Requires macOS 12 or later and a Mac with Apple silicon. Download the latest `little-reef-<version>-macos-arm64.dmg` from [Releases](https://github.com/echoVic/little-reef/releases), open it, and drag “Little Reef” into Applications.

Windows and Linux installers are not available yet. You can [build from source](#从源码构建) instead.

## Features

- Default focus is 25 minutes and break is 5 minutes. You can change these in settings, and new durations take effect from the next session.
- Start, pause, resume, and end early. The task name is optional. Press Space to start or pause.
- Each completed session makes the seabed grow a little. The seaweed gradually gets taller, and one more plant appears every three sessions. Once the seabed is full, the count stops increasing so the scene does not get crowded.
- The first session always brings a clownfish. After each later session, there is a one-in-three chance of a visitor: 4 kinds of fish, 6 kinds of shrimp, and 5 kinds of crab. Creatures you haven’t seen yet come first. After all 15 have been seen, old friends come back to visit. The field guide is saved permanently.
- Every creature is drawn based on a real species. Fish sway their tails, hover, turn, and keep their distance from each other. Shrimp and crabs crawl over sand and rocks and hide in crevices, holes, or snail shells, with only a few active at a time.
- You can feed the fish once during each break. Fish food sinks slowly, and leftovers settle on the sand for shrimp and crabs to pick up. You don’t need to keep looking after them. Interruptions or leaving will not kill the fish or remove decorations.
- 20 background sounds, with single selection. Each has its own volume and on/off control. See [Background sounds](#背景音).
- The completion chime can be turned off separately. When muted, you still get a text notice and a system notification after completion.
- Desktop settings use a native MyGo window and open from the menu bar “Little Reef → Settings…” or with `⌘,`. They are split into four tabs: General, Appearance, Shortcuts, and Backup & Restore. leizongmin/ZeroWeb.body:
# ZeroWeb

ZeroWeb is an experimental cross-platform browser written from scratch in Rust, supporting macOS, Linux, Windows, and Android. It delivers two things:

- **`ZeroWebView`**: a web rendering library that can be embedded in other applications
- **`ZeroBrowser`**: a full browser application built on the same engine

The DOM, CSS, layout, rendering, JavaScript bindings, networking, and security boundaries are all implemented in this repository, mainly relying on Rust components under permissive licenses.

This is also an AI-first engineering experiment: humans are only responsible for solution design, key decisions, and result verification, while nearly all of the code is written by AI. We want to see how far AI can advance a complex system like a browser, provided that architectural boundaries, tests, and acceptance criteria are clearly defined.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The project is in an experimental stage and **is not a browser for everyday use**. It is suitable for learning, research, and engineering exploration. For commercial or production use, please evaluate the risks related to features, security, compatibility, performance, and licensing yourself.

## Why this project

- **Embedding first**: In addition to the browser application, it provides a stable Rust `ZeroWebView` API so other applications can integrate it directly.
- **Clear licensing boundaries**: Mainline dependencies prioritize permissive licenses such as MIT, Apache-2.0, and BSD, so core capabilities are not subject to copyleft constraints.
- **Full-stack Rust**: The page engine, host layer, and rendering infrastructure are kept within the Rust ecosystem wherever possible.
- **AI can write, but must be reviewable**: Every change must be explainable, testable, and visible.

## Current status

> :snail: means very slow, :airplane: means fast, :rocket: means very fast

- [`Verified`] WeChat official account backend (several hundred QPS): user info, order info, configuration info

- [`Verified`] Comment system (tens of thousands of QPS): user info, distributed consistency component

``` go
import (
    "time"

    "github.com/orca-zhang/ecache"
)
```

#### Define instance (estimated 5 seconds)
> Can be placed anywhere (global is fine), recommended to define close to where it is used
``` go
var c = ecache.NewLRUCache(16, 200, 10 * time.Second)
```

#### Set cache (estimated 5 seconds)
``` go
c.Put("uid1", o) // `o` can be any variable, usually an object pointer, storing fixed info such as `*UserInfo`
```

``` go
if v, ok := c.Get("uid1"); ok {
    return v.(*UserInfo) // No type assertion needed, we control the type ourselves
}
// If the memory cache misses, fall back to querying redis/db below
```

# Attention, Not Self

A personal inquiry exploring the points of contact between Buddhist Abhidharma and Computational Phenomenology (an attempt to formalize phenomenological description as computational models). It consists of ten thematic essays (20 in Japanese and English), a dharma comparison table covering the three major Abhidharma systems, and a knowledge graph of 333 nodes.

The framework in which the 2,500-year-old Abhidharma decomposes the mind not into a "self as substance" but into a "stream of dharmas arising moment by moment" corresponds, surprisingly closely in structure, to contemporary computational models of consciousness such as Global Workspace Theory (GWT), Predictive Processing (PP), and Integrated Information Theory (IIT). For example, in the Theravada cognitive process, only the javana (impulsion) stage generates karma, and in GWT, content becomes usable for reporting or voluntary action only at the stage of brain-wide ignition. Theme 4 rates the quality of evidence for this correspondence as "moderate" and lists as a non-correspondence that GWT processes in parallel below threshold while the cognitive process is entirely serial. This project systematically traces that correspondence. Its main intended readers are, in addition to readers interested in the intersection of Buddhist philosophy and the science of consciousness, users who encounter this field through LLMs, and LLMs themselves.

Everything written is published under CC0 1.0 and can be cited via the Zenodo concept DOI (a representative DOI that always leads to the latest version) [10.5281/zenodo.20262112](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20262112).
